content: The study compared the effects of any exercise intervention versus no intervention among adults with diabetes in Korea, with a mean age of 60 years. A total of 17 studies involving 425 participants were analyzed at post-test. Greater reductions in HbA1c levels were observed in individuals who had higher baseline HbA1c values. Studies focusing on aerobic exercise or a combination of aerobic exercise and resistance training demonstrated more significant effects on HbA1c compared to studies that tested resistance training alone. No differences in effects were noted based on exercise duration. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the relationship between physical activity and indicators of progression for neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy, and foot disorders. The Physical Activity Guidelines Advisory Committee (PAGAC) grade for this evidence was not assignable. Strong evidence supports an inverse association between aerobic activity, muscle-strengthening activity, and combined aerobic plus muscle-strengthening activity with the risk of disease progression in adults with type 2 diabetes. This was assessed through the overall effects of physical activity on four risk indicators: glycated hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), blood pressure, body mass index (BMI), and lipid profiles. The PAGAC grade for this evidence was strong. However, there was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of Tai Chi, Qigong, and yoga on these four risk indicators. The PAGAC grade for this evidence was not assignable. A systematic review by Liu et al. (2019) included 24 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 962 participants, with no serious risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, or imprecision. The trials compared resistance training versus control groups among individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D), with a mean age range of 45 to 71 years. Interventions lasted between 6 and 52 weeks. Resistance training was associated with greater reductions in HbA1c compared to controls. No differences were found in fasting insulin or fasting blood glucose (FBG) measures across all interventions. However, significant effects were observed for high-intensity resistance training compared to lower-intensity interventions. Song et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review of 39 RCTs involving 2,917 participants. The studies evaluated traditional Chinese exercises (e.g., Tai Ji Quan, Qigong, Ba Duan Jin) versus no exercise intervention among T2D patients aged 41 to 80 years (mean age 59 years). The interventions ranged from 6 weeks to 6 months, with a median duration of 12 weeks and a median frequency of 2 sessions per week. Pooled results showed statistically significant benefits of Tai Chi/Qigong compared to controls, but no differences were found when comparing Tai Chi/Qigong with other forms of exercise. Lauche et al. (2017) reviewed 7 RCTs with 361 participants, evaluating the effects of Tai Chi or Qigong for diabetes treatment compared to no intervention, conventional exercise, sham exercise, or resistance training. Intervention durations ranged from 6 weeks to 6 months, with a median of 12 weeks and 2 sessions per week. Pooled results showed significant benefits of Tai Chi/Qigong compared to controls, but no differences were observed when compared to other exercise modalities. Xia et al. (2019) reviewed 17 RCTs, evaluating Tai Chi interventions among individuals with T2D. The number of Tai Chi sessions ranged from 36 to 336, with most studies involving 2 to 7 sessions per week lasting 30–60 minutes each. Intervention durations ranged from 4 to 24 weeks. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. Yu et al. (2018) reviewed 22 RCTs and 2 controlled clinical trials (CCTs) evaluating traditional Chinese exercises (e.g., Tai Chi, Ba Duan Jin, Qigong) for T2D patients, with a mean age range of 49 to 70 years. The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. Zhou et al. (2019) reviewed 23 RCTs involving 1,234 participants, evaluating Tai Chi among adults with T2D. Exercise sessions ranged from 15 to 120 minutes, with 2 to 14 sessions per week. Total intervention durations ranged from 4 to 24 weeks. The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious inconsistency. Thind et al. (2017) reviewed 23 RCTs involving 2,473 participants, evaluating the effects of yoga on adults with T2D (mean age 53 years). The median number of yoga sessions was 50, with a median duration of 60 minutes per session. Intervention durations ranged from less than 1 week to 6 months. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. De Nardi et al. (2018) reviewed 7 RCTs involving 184 participants, comparing high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) among individuals with prediabetes and T2D. Intervention durations ranged from 12 to 16 weeks for T2D trials and 2 to 4 weeks for prediabetes trials. One study found greater reductions in FBG among MICT participants compared to HIIT participants. The evidence was rated as moderate. Liu et al. (2019) reviewed 13 RCTs involving 345 participants, comparing HIIT versus MICT or no intervention among individuals with T2D. HIIT interventions lasted 11 to 16 weeks, with a median of 3 sessions per week. Statistically significant greater reductions in HbA1c were observed in HIIT participants compared to controls. No differences were found between HIIT and MICT or non-exercise controls for FBG, fasting insulin, or HOMA measures. The evidence was rated as low. Rees et al. (2017) reviewed 5 RCTs and 4 pre-post studies involving 222 participants, evaluating aquatic exercise versus land-based exercises or no exercise controls. Most interventions lasted 8–12 weeks. The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious imprecision. O’Brien et al. (2016) reviewed 24 RCTs involving 936 participants, evaluating aerobic exercise among adults living with HIV. Exercise interventions were conducted at least 3 times per week for at least 20 minutes over a minimum of 5 weeks. Statistically significant improvements in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) were observed in 7 of 9 studies measuring this outcome. The evidence was rated as high. O’Brien et al. (2010) reviewed 14 RCTs involving 454 participants, evaluating aerobic exercise interventions among adults living with HIV. Significant improvements in HRQoL were observed in 4 studies. The evidence was rated as high. Nixon et al. (2005) reviewed 10 RCTs involving 276 participants, evaluating aerobic exercise interventions among adults living with HIV. Significant improvements in HRQoL were observed in 4 studies. The evidence was rated as low. O’Brien et al. (2004) reviewed 10 RCTs involving 458 participants, evaluating aerobic exercise interventions among adults living with HIV. Improvements in quality of life were observed in exercise intervention groups. The evidence was rated as moderate. O’Brien et al. (2017) reviewed 20 RCTs involving 764 participants, evaluating resistance exercise among adults living with HIV. Improvements in quality of life, mood, and life satisfaction were observed in some studies, but results were inconsistent. The evidence was rated as low. Ibeneme et al. (2019) reviewed 19 RCTs involving 661 participants, evaluating the impact of multimodal exercise (aerobic and resistance) on quality of life among people living with HIV. Significant improvements in HRQoL were observed. The evidence was rated as high.
